how-much-to-charge-for-a-mobile-notary-a.text:
← Notary trip quote

How much should a mobile notary charge for a trip?

The statutory fee per signature is the part that is capped, published, and easy to look up — and on a mobile appointment it is usually the smallest line on the invoice. What actually decides whether the job was worth taking is the drive, the time the drive costs you, and whatever the appointment turns into once you are there. Quoting from the notarial fee alone prices the paperwork and gives the travel away.

Open the free notary trip quote calculator

Build the quote in parts

  1. Mileage: round-trip miles at your per-mile rate.
  2. Travel time and appointment time, both at your hourly rate.
  3. Statutory fees for the signatures involved, plus a fee per witness you supply.
  4. Waiting time at its own rate, and an after-hours surcharge where it applies.
  5. Compare the total with your appointment minimum, and quote whichever is higher.

Worked example

A 20-mile round trip at $0.70 per mile is $14.00 of mileage. Thirty minutes of driving and a 45-minute appointment at $60 per hour add $30.00 and $45.00. State fees of $15.00 and one witness at $25.00 bring the total to $129.00, comfortably above the $50.00 appointment minimum, so the minimum does not apply. Note the shape of it: $44.00 of that quote — more than the notarial and witness fees combined — is travel the capped fee does not cover. Drop the travel lines and the same appointment quotes at $85.00, and the drive is unpaid.

The other question: is this offer worth taking?

Everything above assumes you set the price. Much of the work that fills a signing agent's calendar does not arrive that way — a signing service emails a flat fee already attached: $85, refinance package, 45 miles, 138 pages. There is nothing to quote. The decision is accept, counter, or decline, and the fee on the screen is not the number to decide on.

Two costs decide it, and neither appears in the offer. The first is printing. A loan package is printed twice, once for the borrower and once for the lender, so 138 pages is 276 sheets — paper and toner at roughly $0.04 a sheet is $11.04 gone before you leave the house, and the printing itself is half an hour standing at the machine. The second is the drive, which is not the mileage rate you would have billed: 45 miles at about $0.30 a mile in fuel and wear is $13.50 you actually spend.

So that $85 is $85 minus $24.54 of your own money, over an hour of driving, an hour at the table, and half an hour at the printer — two and a half hours. It pays $24.18 an hour. The same $85 for a ten-minute walk-in three blocks away is a different job at four times the rate, and the offer email makes them look identical.

Two figures are worth knowing before you reply. The walk-away fee is what the job costs you in cash whatever your time is worth — $24.54 here, and below it you are paying to work. The fee that pays your rate covers those costs and then pays your entered hourly rate for every minute the job takes: $174.54. An $85 offer sits between the two, which is exactly what "worth taking on a slow afternoon, worth countering on a full one" looks like in numbers.

Note what the same arithmetic says about your print fee. If billing $0.20 a page does not cover the half hour at the printer at your own hourly rate, the fee that pays your rate lands above your quote — a signal that the print line, not the travel line, is the one priced too low.

Test an offer in the calculator

What varies by state

Statutory per-signature fees are set by your state and are the one line you cannot price yourself. Travel, waiting, and convenience charges are generally not capped the same way, but the rules genuinely differ: some states require the travel fee to be disclosed and agreed separately from the notarial fee, and a few regulate it. Check your own state's notary handbook before you publish a rate card.

Common questions

How much should a mobile notary charge for a trip?

Price it as separate lines rather than one improvised number: mileage at your per-mile rate, travel time at your hourly rate, the appointment itself at that same hourly rate, any statutory per-signature fees, witness fees per witness, waiting time at its own rate, and an after-hours surcharge if it applies. Add them, then compare the total with your appointment minimum and charge whichever is higher. Statutory notarial fees are capped by your state; travel, waiting, and convenience charges generally are not, but the rules differ by state.

Why do I lose money on short notary appointments?

Because the billable part of a mobile appointment is much shorter than the job. A 45-minute signing with a 30-minute round trip is 75 minutes of your day, and the capped per-signature fee covers none of the driving. Quoting from the notarial fee alone prices the paperwork and gives away the travel — which is why an appointment minimum exists: it sets a floor under jobs whose travel and setup cost more than their signatures.

Should I charge for travel time as well as mileage?

They pay for two different things, so most mobile notaries charge both. Mileage covers the vehicle — fuel, wear, and insurance — and is usually set per mile. Travel time covers the hour of your day the drive consumes, which mileage does not compensate at all: a 20-mile trip through city traffic costs far more of your time than 20 highway miles. Pricing them as separate lines also makes the quote easier to explain to a client who asks why a nearby signing costs less.

Is an $85 loan signing worth taking?

It depends almost entirely on the drive and the page count, which the offer does not mention. Take $85 for a 138-page package 45 miles away: printed twice that is 276 sheets, about $11.04 in paper and toner, plus roughly $13.50 of fuel and wear for the round trip — $24.54 of your own money. The job occupies an hour of driving, an hour at the table and half an hour at the printer, so what is left works out at $24.18 an hour. The identical $85 for a ten-minute walk-in nearby pays four times that. Decide on the hourly figure, not the fee.

How much does printing a loan signing package actually cost?

More than most agents bill for it, because the package is printed twice — the borrower's set and the lender's set — and because the time is invisible. At roughly $0.04 a sheet for paper and toner, a 138-page package printed twice costs about $11.04 in consumables, and printing and collating it is commonly 20 to 40 minutes. Bill printing as a per-page fee rather than folding it into the appointment rate, and check that fee against the time: if $0.20 a page does not cover half an hour of your hourly rate, the print line is subsidising the client.

How should I quote waiting time at a signing?

Quote it in advance as its own rate, usually lower than your working hourly rate, and say up front when it starts — typically after a stated grace period past the appointment time. Waiting for a late signer, a missing witness, or documents that have not arrived is the most common way a booked appointment overruns, and a rate agreed beforehand turns an awkward conversation at the kitchen table into a line the client already accepted.

Common questions

Why bill mileage and drive time separately?

They cover different real costs. Mileage pays for the vehicle — fuel and wear — while drive time pays for the hour you are not earning your appointment rate. At the defaults that is $14 (20 round-trip miles × $0.70) plus $30 (30 minutes at a $60/hour rate) — two separate line items totaling $44 before a single form is notarized.

When does the minimum appointment fee actually apply?

Only when travel, appointment time, waiting, and fees add up to less than the minimum. At the defaults the trip already totals $129, well above the $50 minimum, so it never triggers here — it exists to protect a short, nearby signing (say, a five-minute drive and one document) from quoting below what driving out at all is worth.

Why is each witness priced separately instead of a flat notarization fee?

Because each extra witness usually means extra identification checks and signature lines, not a fixed add-on. The calculator multiplies the per-witness fee by the witness count, so a two-witness will costs twice the $25 default witness fee rather than one flat rider charge regardless of how many people are signing.

How is waiting time different from appointment time?

Appointment time is the notarization itself, billed at your hourly rate. Waiting time is time spent on-site but not actively working — for a signer running late, or documents still being printed — and it can be billed at its own, often lower, waiting rate rather than assuming every minute on-site is worth the full hourly fee.

Why does printing get its own charge and its own cost?

Because one is money coming in and the other is money going out, and they are different numbers. A 138-page loan package printed twice is 276 sheets: billed at $0.20 a page that is $55.20 of the fee, while the paper and toner cost about $0.04 a page, or $11.04 out of your pocket. Collapsing them into one figure hides whether your print fee actually covers your printer. Print time is counted separately again — it is 20 to 40 minutes you cannot sell to anyone else — but it is never billed at your hourly rate on top of the per-page charge, because that would bill the same work twice.

A signing service is offering me a flat fee. How do I know if it is worth taking?

Compare it to what is left per hour, not to the fee. Enter the offer and the calculator subtracts what you actually spend — paper, toner, fuel — and divides by every hour the job occupies, including the drive, the wait and the time at the printer. An $85 signing 45 miles away with a 138-page package prints 276 sheets, costs $24.54 out of pocket, and takes two and a half hours: $24.18 an hour, not $85. The same $85 for a ten-minute walk-in is a different job entirely.

What is the difference between the walk-away fee and the fee that pays my rate?

The walk-away fee is what the job costs you in cash before your time is worth anything — paper, toner and fuel. Below it you are paying to work. The fee that pays your rate is higher: it covers those costs and then pays the hourly rate you entered for every minute the job takes, with waiting valued at your waiting rate. On the worked signing above those are $24.54 and $174.54, so an $85 offer is above the first and well below the second — worth taking on a slow day, worth countering on a full one.

Is my client's appointment information uploaded anywhere?

No. The quote is calculated entirely in your browser and your entries are saved only to this browser's local storage so the form remembers them next time — nothing is sent to a server. Anonymous feature counting can be turned off with the button in the footer, and it is already skipped when your browser sends Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control.

vs-doing-the-trip-math-yourself.html.text:
← Notary Trip Quote

This calculator vs. doing the trip math yourself

Mileage times a rate, plus a flat fee, is the estimate most mobile notaries do in their head while an offer is sitting in a text message. It's usually not wrong so much as incomplete — it's the four or five lines beyond mileage that get dropped under time pressure, and those are often the lines that decide whether the trip is worth taking.

What each approach actually does

Doing the math yourself works well for the part that's simple: miles times a per-mile rate. Where it tends to go wrong is everything past that — a 100-200 page loan package printed in two sets has a printing charge and a separate printing cost that both need tracking, a witness fee applies only when the signing needs one, waiting time only shows up if the borrower is late or a page is missing, and an evening or weekend appointment carries an after-hours premium that's easy to forget applying consistently. None of those individually breaks the math. Missing two or three of them on the same trip does.

This calculator holds all nine lines — travel miles and minutes, appointment labor, a minimum fee, state-set signing fees, witness fees, after-hours work, waiting time, and print charge and cost — so nothing gets dropped because the phone buzzed mid estimate. It also computes the one number head math almost never reaches: the effective hourly rate once vehicle cost is subtracted from mileage revenue, which is what actually tells you whether a flat offered fee clears the bar.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Is $0.70 a mile times 45 miles roughly right?Either way — that part of a mental estimate is usually fine.
Does the offer still clear my target rate after printing two 138-page sets, one witness, and a 30-minute wait?This calculator — those four lines are easy to drop from a mental estimate and each one moves the total.
What's my real hourly rate on this trip once vehicle cost comes out of the mileage revenue?This calculator's effective-hourly-rate figure, not a rough per-mile subtraction.
Why does an $85 flat offer 45 miles away sometimes pay less than minimum wage?This calculator's own trip-pricing walkthrough.
Is a quick mental estimate fine for a short local job with no witnesses or printing?Yes — on a simple trip the two approaches land close to the same number.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Isn't multiplying miles by a rate close enough?

For the mileage line alone, yes — that part of the head-math estimate is usually right. What it leaves out is everything mileage doesn't cover: the printing charge and cost for a 100-200 page loan package printed in two sets, the vehicle cost per mile that actually eats into the mileage revenue rather than adding to it, witness fees when the signing needs one or two, waiting time when the borrower is late or a page is missing, and the after-hours premium on an evening or weekend appointment. Each of those is easy to forget under time pressure and each one moves the real number away from the quick estimate.

What does this calculator do that a rough estimate can't?

It holds all nine cost lines at once — travel, appointment labor, the minimum fee, state-set signing fees, witnesses, after-hours work, waiting time, and both the print charge and the separate print cost — and turns them into two numbers a mental estimate rarely reaches: the total quote, and the effective hourly rate once vehicle cost is subtracted from the mileage revenue. That second number is the one that tells you whether an offered flat fee is actually worth the drive, not just whether it sounds reasonable.

When is a quick mental estimate the better choice?

When the trip is simple enough that none of the missed lines apply — a short local trip, no witnesses, no printing, daytime, no waiting — a rough estimate and this calculator will land close to the same number, and typing it in may not be worth the twenty seconds. The calculator earns its keep on the trip that isn't simple: a 45-mile package job with two witnesses and an evening appointment, where the lines that are easy to forget are also the ones that decide whether the offer clears your target hourly rate.

This calculator vs. NotaryGadget

Two different shapes: NotaryGadget is a subscription platform for running a notary's whole book of appointments, mileage, and tax records. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one trip cost, and does the offered fee actually clear it, before you confirm the appointment.

What each tool is for

NotaryGadget is a subscription platform built specifically for loan signing agents. It tracks appointments, mileage, and expenses across a notary's whole calendar, generates invoices, and exports the records a 1099 filing needs at year end. NotaryGadget's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — notary-specific scheduling and bookkeeping software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for NotaryGadget appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what NotaryGadget does. It does not track a calendar, generate a 1099 export, or hold a record across jobs. It takes one trip — travel miles and drive time, appointment labor, a minimum fee, state-set signing fees, witness fees, after-hours work, waiting time, and print costs — and turns that into what the trip should cost, the effective hourly rate once vehicle cost is subtracted, and whether a signing service's flat offered fee actually clears that number. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

They do different jobs, and a mobile notary of any size may end up using both.
